subject: How to explain the std.all, std.lv and std.nox were NAs

messages.author: d8517e92c7758dc2
messages.subject: How to explain the std.all, std.lv and std.nox were NAs
parts:
Hi Professors, 

I would like to ask one question about the estimates from the latent growth model. I fit a biraviate latent growth model with cross-lagged effect, for the latent growth intercept and slope, I also fit them to regress on some time-independent variables, however, some of the standardard estimates were NAs, like this below: 



I would like to ask how to explain the NA results in the table. 

One more question is: in my bivariate latent growth model with cross-lagged effect, the two constructs are in quite different scales, for example, one (denoted as Ai) ranges from 80-200, and the other (denoted as Bi) ranges from 0.01-0.5, shall I rescale them to a similar scales, for example, Ai/100 and Bi*10? If I don't change the original scale, will this cause the issue of model unconvergence or will lead to some errors for the estimates of the model? 

Thank you very much. 

Regards 

Xueying

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How to explain the std.all, std.lv and std.nox were NAs
parts: some of the standardard estimates were NAs
Where are the rest of your estimates?  Hard to guess, but maybe there is a Heywood case preventing standardization of those particular parameters.  Negative slope variance?
shall I rescale them to a similar scales, for example, Ai/100 and Bi*10?

Sure, that could help prevent convergence problems, if you had any.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: d8517e92c7758dc2
messages.subject: Re: How to explain the std.all, std.lv and std.nox were NAs
parts:
Hi Terrence, 

Thank you very much for your reply. 

I attached the full result, and you are right that some of the variance and covariance are negative (I didn't even notice that). So, how to interpret the negative variance? Not sure if it's a big issue for the model. 

For rescaling the constructs, I have tried to do the rescaling thing, and more results were released (also including different results, for example some significant associations before scaling became non-significant after rescaling, however, the model fit improved after rescaling). I only have one concern that it might be hard to interpret the results, for example, I rescaled the blood pressure by dividing by 100, then the association would be explained as every 100 mmHg blood pressure increasing associated with XX increasing of something else. So I would like to ask whether convergence is the first thing we need to consider when fitting the models. Please forgive me if my question is so stupid. 

Thank you very much again. 

Xueying

messages.author: 12fdd832cacb825e
messages.subject: Re: How to explain the std.all, std.lv and std.nox were NAs
parts:
Xueying,

As far as rescaling, to be blunt, convergence is mandatory, but easy interpretability is optional. But it's not as bad as you're thinking. In your example, you would run the analysis with the rescaled mmHg, but report it after multiplying the regression coefficient (and its standard error / confidence limits) by 100 to get it back in original scale.

Pat
